questions.stem: Eliza, 32, is seated in a GP room with her neck exposed. You can see a smooth midline swelling in the lower anterior neck. Before you palpate from behind, you want to show the examiner that the swelling is thyroid in origin. What do you ask her to do while you watch the swelling?
options: Stick out her tongue while you watch the swelling
Raise both arms above her head and hold them there
Turn her head against your hand, first to one side
Take a sip of water, hold it, then swallow
questions.why: The thyroid sits inside the pretracheal fascia, which is attached to the larynx, so a goitre rises when she swallows. Giving her water makes the swallow easy to see. A thyroglossal cyst instead rises when she sticks out her tongue.
notes: Rising on tongue protrusion picks out a thyroglossal duct cyst. It does not confirm a thyroid gland swelling, which moves with swallowing.
Raising the arms is Pemberton's manoeuvre, which looks for a retrosternal goitre blocking the thoracic inlet. It does not show where a neck swelling comes from.
Turning the head against resistance tenses sternocleidomastoid, which helps place lateral neck lumps. It does not separate a thyroid swelling from other midline lumps.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, has new thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation at about 110/min. She is haemodynamically stable with no chest pain or heart failure, and has no asthma, hypertension, diabetes or vascular disease. You are seeing her in general practice. What is the most appropriate plan for her atrial fibrillation now?
options: Propranolol for rate control, no anticoagulant, expect reversion once euthyroid
Start apixaban and arrange electrical cardioversion within the next 48 hours
Oral amiodarone loading to restore sinus rhythm before starting carbimazole
Digoxin for rate control plus aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prevention
questions.why: Thyrotoxic AF is rate-controlled with a beta blocker such as propranolol, which also eases adrenergic symptoms, and it usually reverts once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so she needs no anticoagulant now. Cardioversion waits until she is euthyroid.
notes: With CHA2DS2-VA 0 she does not need an anticoagulant, and cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic is likely to fail or the AF will come back. Cardioversion is deferred until she is euthyroid.
Amiodarone carries a large iodine load and can itself cause thyroid dysfunction. It would worsen and complicate her thyrotoxicosis and delay radioiodine.
Digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxicosis because of high sympathetic tone and faster clearance, and aspirin is no longer recommended to prevent stroke in AF.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, has Graves' disease with gritty, watering eyes. On examination she has exophthalmos, which you can see from the side and from above her head. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Which mechanism best explains why her eyes are pushed forward?
options: Sympathetic overactivity contracting the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle
TSH receptor antibodies activating orbital fibroblasts, swelling muscles and fat
Excess thyroid hormone raising orbital blood flow and causing venous congestion
Anti-TPO antibodies fixing complement within the extraocular muscle fibres
questions.why: TRAb activates TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts, together with IGF-1 receptor signalling. The fibroblasts lay down glycosaminoglycans and make new fat, so the extraocular muscles and orbital fat swell inside the rigid bony orbit and push the eye forward. This is specific to Graves' disease and smoking makes it worse.
notes: Adrenergic overactivity of Müller's muscle causes lid retraction and lid lag, which beta blockers can improve. It does not push the eye forward.
Proptosis does not come from thyroid hormone itself. It can appear or get worse even when the patient is euthyroid, and it does not occur in other causes of thyrotoxicosis.
Anti-TPO antibodies are markers of autoimmune thyroiditis, also found in Hashimoto's disease. They are not the cause of the orbital tissue swelling.

questions.stem: Eliza, 32, asks what would happen if her Graves' disease comes back after carbimazole. You explain that total thyroidectomy is one option, with a risk to a nerve that runs in or near the tracheo-oesophageal groove, close to the inferior thyroid artery. If injured on one side, this nerve leaves her with a hoarse voice. Which nerve is it?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and passes close to the inferior thyroid artery. It supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except cricothyroid, so injury on one side paralyses that vocal cord and causes hoarseness. Injury on both sides can obstruct the airway.
notes: The external branch runs with the superior thyroid artery to the upper pole and supplies cricothyroid. Injury causes voice fatigue and loss of high pitch, not a paralysed vocal cord.
The internal branch is sensory to the larynx above the vocal cords. It enters through the thyrohyoid membrane, well above the gland, so it is rarely at risk in thyroidectomy.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles and can be divided during surgery without changing the voice.
